Q: HiveAccessControlException Permission Denied: user does not have [ALL] privilege A:

I had a similar issue. You may want to check Ranger > Audit > Plugin Status to see if the policy is being applied. If it's not it may be that you have a jersey-client classpath conflict. More details here: https://jonmorisissqlblog.blogspot.com/2021/06/ranger-hive-policy-activation-time.html

Q: DCOM got error "2147942405" from the computer x.x.x.x when attempting to activate the server: A:

According to MS Technet:

https://social.technet.microsoft.com/Forums/Azure/en-US/8bb5807f-73ba-4092-abc8-283d8fced6c4/request-a-certificate-from-certificate-service-fails-dcom-error-2147942405?forum=winserversecurity

With my VERY limited understanding of Certificate servers you may have one of the scenarios:

  1. Client PC's are trying to connect to a Certificate server that no longer exists
  2. Client PC's have a certificate that is valid but the Certificate server no longer exists
  3. A Certificate server is broken
  4. Clients do not have the proper authority to request the Certificate

I say this is limited knowledge as I am currently trying to remove AD Certificate services from a Domain Controller and I can see that in the System event log the exact same messages are being logged as I have stopped the Certificate services to asses the impact. If I get further information I will post back.

Q: Best way to conver HTML content in to PDF A:

Short version: for a WPF app with existing HTML+CSS, WebView2 is the most self-contained free route — it both renders and prints. Reach for PuppeteerSharp/Playwright if you want standalone Chromium, or a dedicated library like SelectPdf for fine-grained in-process PDF control. Skip wkhtmltopdf for new code, and don't reach for QuestPDF/iText unless you're willing to rebuild the layout in code. Details below.

There are really two separate problems here — rendering HTML+CSS to PDF, and printing the result — so I'll split them.

Rendering: pick an engine that actually speaks modern CSS

Your options fall into two camps:

  • Browser-engine renderers (real Chromium/WebKit) — these give you the CSS fidelity you already see in a browser: WebView2, PuppeteerSharp, Playwright, and dedicated converters. Use one of these when you have existing HTML+CSS and want it to look the same.
  • Code-layout libraries — QuestPDF and (mostly) iText7 build the document from C#/limited HTML. QuestPDF does not take arbitrary HTML+CSS at all (you'd rebuild the layout in its fluent API), and iText7's pdfHTML supports only a subset of CSS. Great libraries, wrong tool if your source of truth is HTML+CSS.

A quick honest rundown of the browser-engine options:

Option CSS support Notes
WebView2 Excellent (Edge/Chromium) Free, likely already available in a WPF app; needs the WebView2 Runtime. Can render and print (below).
PuppeteerSharp / Playwright Excellent (Chromium) Bundles a ~Chromium download; heavier; first call is slow (cold start).
wkhtmltopdf / DinkToPdf Dated (old QtWebKit) No modern flexbox/grid, effectively abandoned, native-lib quirks. I'd avoid it for new work.
SelectPdf Good (Chromium-based engine) Windows .NET library with explicit A4 / page-break / margin control.

A4 + pagination caveats (where most of the time actually goes)

Regardless of engine:

  • Drive layout from print CSS: @media print { ... } and @page { size: A4; margin: 15mm; }.
  • Control breaks with page-break-inside: avoid; (or break-inside: avoid;) on rows/cards, and page-break-before/after for forced breaks.
  • If backgrounds/colors drop out, enable print-background graphics (-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; plus the engine's print-background flag).
  • Set the render width to A4 at 96 DPI (~794px) so the browser doesn't lay out wide and then scale.

With SelectPdf specifically, A4 is the default (PdfPageSize.A4); margins are Options.MarginTop/Bottom/Left/Right, and if you ever need everything on one page instead of A4 pagination there's Options.GenerateSinglePagePdf = true.

Printing

If you use WebView2 you don't need a second tool — it prints silently to a named printer:

var settings = webView.CoreWebView2.Environment.CreatePrintSettings();
settings.PrinterName = "Your Printer";
await webView.CoreWebView2.PrintAsync(settings);   // silent, no dialog

If you produced the PDF with a library instead, print it with a PDF renderer (e.g. PdfiumViewer + System.Drawing.Printing.PrintDocument) or a silent-print helper (SumatraPDF -print-to, PDFtoPrinter). Piping raw PDF bytes to the spooler only works if the printer speaks PostScript/PDF, which most desktop printers don't — so render-then-print is the reliable path.

Disclosure: I work on SelectPdf.

Q: openssl sha256sum hash contains output file as part of input when using find command to list the files A:

My two cents:

Alternatively, as this question is tagged bash and while your directory will hold only regular files and directories, you could use bash's wildcards and the extglob bash option, instead of find with -maxdepth 1!!

In an interactive bash session, the following oneliner will generate a sub-shell before cd so your shell session will return to original working dir on exit:

( cd "/some/path/" && sha256sum !(hashedoutput.sha256) >hashedoutput.sha256 )

You could quietly ignore messages like: sha256sum: ...: Is a directory

( cd "/some/path" && LC_ALL=C sha256sum !(hashedoutput.sha256) >hashedoutput.sha256  \
    2> >(grep -v '^sha256sum: .*: Is a directory$' >&2) )

Note: As bash command line's length limit is far away from standard used by find command, this run mostly only one fork to sha256sum, instead of your initial syntax which implie at least two fork and maybe more if number of file to proceed are something big (more infos at Progress bar for grep in bash where before parallelizing grep, using bash only, instead of forking to find, is already quicker).

In a script, you could create a function like:

shopt -s extglob
gen_sha256sum() {
    pushd >/dev/null "$1" || return 1
    sha256sum !(hashedoutput.sha256) >hashedoutput.sha256
    popd >/dev/null
}

In a dedicated bash script file

#!/bin/bash
shopt -s extglob

hashFile="hashedoutput.sha256"

cd "$1" || exit 1
LC_ALL=C sha256sum !("$hashFile") >"$hashFile" 2> >(
    sed -ue '/^sha256sum:.*: Is a directory$/d' >&2 )

Note:

  • sed command on STDERR will drop only line matching: sha256sum: ...: Is a directory! (sed is something lighter and quicker than grep for this kind of job.)
  • Prepanding sed by LC_ALL=C will ensure error message to be printed in english (C), for matching regular expression.

About hidden files

Notice: This will not process on hidden files (having name begin by a dot). If you want to include them, you have to add: .* on sha256sum command line:

shopt -s extglob
gen_sha256sum() {
    pushd >/dev/null "$1" || return 1
    sha256sum !(hashedoutput.sha256) .* >hashedoutput.sha256
    popd >/dev/null
}

or

( cd "/some/path/" && sha256sum !(hashedoutput.sha256) .* >hashedoutput.sha256 )

Limitation

As this will work on any directory entries, this could generate harmnless error trying to access directories. But if your directory hold special entries, like devices, fifos or socket, this could hang. (or worst if run as root user)!

Q: Flutter SDK in Visual Studio Code not working A:

The bin folder belongs to the Flutter SDK, not to a Flutter project. A newly created Flutter app should normally contain folders like lib, android, ios, test, and a pubspec.yaml file.

If your project is empty, likely that the project creation didn't complete successfully. Try running " flutter doctor -v " To check your Flutter installation, then create a new project from the terminal using " flutter create my_app " To see if the same issue occurs.

If the problem persists, please update your question with the output of " flutter doctor -v ", your operating system, and a screenshot of the project structure in VS Code. That will make it easier to identify the cause.
